mainTopic: Reward outweighs punishment; the ban on 'outside books' and on ספר בן סירא, with its good sayings that may still be taught; and many readings of the פסוק 'all the days of the poor are bad.'
overview: The amud opens by finishing a proof that God's measure of good is bigger than His measure of punishment: the מן came through the 'doors' of heaven, but the מבול came only through 'windows.' It then asks how anyone could survive the endless fire in ישעיהו. The answer is that God gives the wicked strength to bear their punishment, and gives the righteous strength to receive their reward. Next the גמרא turns to רבי עקיבא's warning in the משנה about reading 'outside books,' which a ברייתא explains as books of מינים. רב יוסף adds that ספר בן סירא is also forbidden. אביי tests one line from it after another (the fish skin, the daughters, worry, crowds in the house) and shows each matches the תורה or חז"ל, until a list of silly sayings about beards and cups is left as the real problem. רב יוסף concludes that the book's good sayings may still be taught, and he quotes many of them. Finally, several אמוראים explain the פסוק 'all the days of the poor are bad' in different ways: about תלמוד and משנה scholars, a bad or good wife, a sensitive or easygoing person, and a compassionate or cruel person. רבי יהושע בן לוי's reading begins here and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Good is bigger than punishment: doors versus windows
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that מדה טובה is greater than מדת פורענות. It proves this from the 'doors of heaven' used for the מן versus the 'windows of heaven' used for the מבול.
steps.simpleTranslation: So you must say that God's measure of good is greater than His measure of punishment. About good, the verse says He opened the 'doors of heaven' to rain down מן. About punishment, at the מבול, it says only that the 'windows of heaven' were opened.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is wrapping up an argument from just before this section. It states the conclusion: God's goodness is bigger than His punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Doors are much bigger openings than windows. When God gave food (the מן), the פסוק describes doors opening. When He punished (the מבול), the פסוק describes only windows. The size of the opening shows that reward flows in a larger measure than punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: You must say / the conclusion must be

steps.whyThisMatters: This idea, that reward is greater than punishment, is the background for the next question about how people can withstand what they receive.

phrases.aramaic: הֱוֵי אוֹמֵר: מִדָּה טוֹבָה מְרוּבָּה מִמִּדַּת פּוּרְעָנוּת.
phrases.english: You must say: the measure of good is greater than the measure of punishment.
Regarding the measure of good it is written:
"He commanded the skies above,
and opened the doors of heaven,
and rained upon them manna to eat,"
and regarding the measure of punishment it says:
"And the windows of heaven were opened."
phrases.notes: בראשית 7:11, about the flood. Windows are smaller than doors, and that is the whole point.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes an argument that began just before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: God's measure of good is greater than His measure of punishment, as shown by doors versus windows.

steps.title: A verse about endless fire for the wicked
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a פסוק in ישעיהו about the wicked, whose fire will never go out. This sets up a question.
steps.simpleTranslation: About punishment it is written: 'They will go out and see the bodies of the people who rebelled against Me. Their worm will not die, their fire will not go out, and they will be disgusting to all people.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק describing never-ending punishment for the wicked. It is setting up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key words are 'their fire will not go out.' The punishment lasts forever. This raises the problem of how a body could survive such fire, which the next step asks.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who rebel / sin on purpose

phrases.english: Regarding the measure of punishment it is written:
"And they shall go out and look upon the corpses of the men
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 66:24

phrases.english: who rebelled against Me,
for their worm shall not die
and their fire shall not be put out,
and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from comparing good and punishment to looking closely at a verse about punishment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wicked are punished with a fire that never goes out.

steps.title: How can anyone survive endless fire?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that in this world a finger put into fire is burned at once. So how could the wicked last in a fire that never stops?
steps.simpleTranslation: But when a person puts his finger into fire in this world, he is burned right away!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem with the פסוק. A person can't even survive a moment in fire, so how can he survive fire forever?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge comes from ordinary experience. Fire destroys a body almost instantly. An endless punishment by fire seems impossible, because the person would be gone right away.

phrases.english: But doesn't a person who puts out his finger
into the fire in this world
get burned immediately!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how the punishment in the verse from step 2 could actually work.
steps.kashyaTarget: The verse's description of a fire that never goes out on the wicked.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fire burns a person immediately, so no one could last in an endless fire.

steps.title: God gives strength to receive both punishment and reward
steps.stepSummary: God gives the wicked special strength to endure their punishment. In the same way, He gives the righteous special strength to receive their huge reward.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, just as God gives the wicked strength to take their punishment, so too God gives the righteous strength to take their reward.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: God gives a person the strength to bear what he receives. It then applies the same idea to the reward of the righteous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer is that normal human limits don't apply here, because God supplies the needed strength. The גמרא then flips the idea to the good side. The reward of the righteous is so great that they would also need God-given strength to hold it. This ties back to step 1, where good is greater than punishment.
steps.whatToRemember: God gives strength to the wicked to bear punishment and to the righteous to receive their reward, which is greater.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, כְּשֵׁם שֶׁנּוֹתֵן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
phrases.english: Rather, just as the Holy One, Blessed be He, gives
strength to the wicked to receive their punishment,
so too the Holy One, Blessed be He, gives
strength to the righteous to receive their reward.
phrases.notes: This points back to the huge reward the גמרא described just before this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, כְּשֵׁם שֶׁנּוֹתֵן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא כֹּחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains that God supplies supernatural strength.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A human body could not survive endless fire.
steps.terutzMaskana: God gives the wicked strength to endure, and likewise gives the righteous strength to receive their reward.

steps.title: The משנה: reading outside books
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה. There רבי עקיבא says that one who reads 'outside books' also loses his share in עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: also one who reads the outside books, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה. It is setting up an explanation of what 'outside books' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists people who have no share in עולם הבא. רבי עקיבא adds someone who reads 'outside books.' The term is unclear, so the גמרא will define it next.

keyTerms.meaning: Outside books (books outside the accepted holy writings)

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
Also one who reads the outside books, etc.
phrases.notes: The 'etc.' is the rest of the משנה's line: such a person has no share in the World to Come.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: אַף הַקּוֹרֵא בַּסְּפָרִים הַחִיצוֹנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic: the גמרא returns to the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who reads outside books loses his share in עולם הבא.

steps.title: Outside books means books of heretics
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that 'outside books' means ספרי מינים, the books of heretics.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: this means books of heretics.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that tells us what the משנה means by 'outside books.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forbidden books are not just any books other than the holy ones. They are specifically heretical books, written by מינים.

phrases.english: It was taught: this means books of heretics.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the משנה's term from step 5.

steps.title: רב יוסף: ספר בן סירא is also forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says that it is also forbidden to read ספר בן סירא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: it is also forbidden to read the book of בן סירא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף adds another book to the forbidden list: ספר בן סירא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ספר בן סירא is not a book of מינים. Even so, רב יוסף forbids reading it. This raises the question of why, which אביי asks next.

keyTerms.meaning: The book of בן סירא (a book of wisdom sayings)

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
in the book of Ben Sira
it is also forbidden to read.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר: בְּסֵפֶר בֶּן סִירָא נָמֵי אָסוּר לְמִיקְרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the list of forbidden books beyond step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Reading ספר בן סירא is forbidden.

steps.title: אביי asks why: the fish-skin saying
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רב יוסף for his reason. He suggests one possible reason: בן סירא wrote a strange piece of advice about not skinning a fish.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: what is the reason? If you say it is because he wrote in it: 'Don't strip the skin off a fish from its ear, so the skin won't go to waste. Instead roast it in the fire and eat it with two loaves.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רב יוסף by asking what is wrong with ספר בן סירא. He offers a first possible reason, a strange line about fish, so that he can test it in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggestion is that this saying looks silly or pointless, so the book should not be read. אביי raises this reason only in order to knock it down. The question 'what is the reason' works as a challenge to רב יוסף's ruling.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: what is the reason?
If you say it is because he wrote [in it]:
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording; some printings leave it out.

phrases.english: Do not strip the skin of the fish from its ear,
so that its skin does not go to waste,
rather, roast it in the fire
and eat two loaves with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: מַאי טַעְמָא? אִילֵּימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the reason behind רב יוסף's ruling in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's ban on ספר בן סירא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the reason is this fish saying, it is not a good enough reason. The next steps show this.

steps.title: Read simply, the Torah says the same
steps.stepSummary: If the fish line is read simply, it just teaches not to waste things. The תורה itself teaches that too, with 'do not destroy its trees.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If you object to its simple meaning, the תורה also wrote: 'Do not destroy its trees.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי rejects the first way the fish line could be a problem. Read simply, it says nothing wrong, since the תורה also forbids pointless waste.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The simple message of the fish line is 'don't ruin something useful.' That is the same value as the תורה's command not to destroy fruit trees. So the line can't be the reason to ban the book.

phrases.english: If it is from its simple meaning,
in the Torah it is also written:
"Do not destroy its trees."
phrases.notes: דברים 20:19

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Knocks down the first possible way of reading the fish line from step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the simple reading as grounds for banning the book.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The simple meaning matches the תורה's own value of not wasting things.

steps.title: Read as a hint, it teaches proper conduct
steps.stepSummary: If the fish line is read as a hint (דרש), it teaches proper marital conduct. A husband should not have relations with his wife in an unnatural way. That is also fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you object to its hinted meaning, it is teaching us proper conduct: a man should not have relations with his wife in an unnatural way.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי rejects the second way the fish line could be a problem. Even read as a hint, it teaches good behavior.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some read the fish line as a hidden hint about marriage. Read that way, it teaches דרך ארץ, proper and caring conduct between husband and wife. Either way, simple or hinted, the line is not a reason to forbid the book.
steps.whatToRemember: אביי shows that the fish saying in ספר בן סירא is fine whether read simply or as a hint. So it cannot be רב יוסף's reason for the ban.

phrases.english: If it is from its interpretation,
he is teaching us proper conduct:
that one should not have relations in an unnatural way.
phrases.notes: He means a husband with his wife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Knocks down the second possible way of reading the fish line, completing the rejection begun in step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the hinted reading as grounds for banning the book.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The hinted meaning teaches proper marital conduct, not anything objectionable.

steps.title: Maybe the problem is the line about daughters
steps.stepSummary: אביי suggests another possible reason for banning בן סירא: a passage describing a daughter as a constant source of worry for her father.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, maybe the problem is that it says: 'A daughter is a false treasure for her father. Out of fear for her he cannot sleep at night. When she is little, he fears she will be seduced. As a young girl, he fears she will act immorally. When grown, he fears she won't marry. Once married, he fears she won't have children. When old, he fears she will practice witchcraft.'
steps.whatsHappening: The fish line was cleared, so the גמרא tries a new guess about what is wrong with ספר בן סירא. It quotes a harsh-sounding passage about daughters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that this passage puts down daughters and might upset fathers of girls. If so, that could be a reason to ban the book. The next step will test this guess.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, because it is written. Introduces a new guess about the reason.
A false treasure: something that looks precious but brings worry
In her childhood, when she is a minor
She has become a fully grown woman

phrases.english: Rather, because it is written:
phrases.notes: אביי is still guessing at רב יוסף's reason. 'It is written' here means in ספר בן סירא.

phrases.english: "A daughter is for her father a false treasure;
out of fear for her he will not sleep at night:
when she is a minor, lest she be seduced;
as a young girl, lest she act immorally;
once she is grown, lest she not marry;

phrases.aramaic: נִישֵּׂאת – שֶׁמָּא לֹא יִהְיוּ לָהּ בָּנִים,
phrases.english: once she marries, lest she have no children;
once she grows old, lest she practice witchcraft."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the fish line was cleared in steps 9-10, אביי offers a new possible reason for the ban.
steps.kashyaTarget: The permissibility of reading ספר בן סירא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A passage that speaks harshly about daughters might be a reason to forbid the book.

steps.title: The Sages said the same about daughters
steps.stepSummary: The guess is pushed away: רבנן themselves said that it is a blessing to have sons and hard to have daughters, even though the world needs both.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the Sages also said this: 'The world cannot exist without males and without females. Still, happy is the one whose children are sons, and woe to the one whose children are daughters.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the daughter guess. רבנן said something very similar, so this line cannot be the reason the book is banned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea that raising daughters brings extra worry already appears in a saying of רבנן. Since חז"ל say it themselves, the line in בן סירא is not a problem. So the search for רב יוסף's reason goes on.

phrases.english: But the Sages also said it:
It is impossible for the world to exist
without males and without females.
Happy is one whose children are males,
and woe to one whose children are females.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the guess from step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The daughter passage as a reason for the ban
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבנן expressed the same idea, so it cannot be what makes the book forbidden.

steps.title: Maybe the problem is the line about worry
steps.stepSummary: אביי tries a third guess: a line in בן סירא that warns against letting worry into your heart because worry has killed strong men.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, maybe the problem is that it says: 'Do not let worry into your heart, for worry has killed mighty men.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes another guess about why the book is banned. It quotes בן סירא's advice not to let worry take over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether this advice is something חז"ל would object to. The next step answers by comparing it to a פסוק.

phrases.english: Rather, because it is written:
"Do not bring worry into your heart,
for worry has killed mighty men."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the daughter guess was rejected, a new guess is offered.
steps.kashyaTarget: The permissibility of reading ספר בן סירא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Perhaps this advice about worry is the objectionable content that justifies the ban.

steps.title: שלמה said the same about worry
steps.stepSummary: The guess is rejected: שלמה already wrote in משלי that worry weighs a person down.
steps.simpleTranslation: But שלמה said it too: 'Worry in a man's heart weighs him down.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the worry guess. A פסוק in משלי, written by שלמה, says almost the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If תנ"ך itself teaches that worry is harmful, then בן סירא saying the same cannot be a problem. The next step explains how to read the פסוק so it fully matches בן סירא's advice.

keyTerms.meaning: Bows him down, weighs him down

phrases.english: But שלמה said it:
"Worry in a man's heart weighs him down."
phrases.notes: משלי 12:25

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the guess from step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The worry line as a reason for the ban
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A פסוק in משלי already says the same thing.

steps.title: Two ways to read the word ישחנה
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי and רבי אסי read the word ישחנה as advice for handling worry. One says to push it out of your mind, and the other says to talk it over with others.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי and רבי אסי disagree. One says the פסוק means: let him push the worry out of his mind. The other says: let him talk about it with other people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two אמוראים who explain the word ישחנה in the פסוק. Both readings turn it into advice for getting rid of worry, just like בן סירא's line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, the פסוק says that worry weighs a person down. רבי אמי and רבי אסי read the word as an instruction for what to do about it, either by forgetting the worry or by sharing it. Either way, the פסוק teaches the same thing as בן סירא, which makes the rejection in step 14 even stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him remove it from his mind
Let him talk it over with others

phrases.english: רבי אמי and רבי אסי:
One said: let him push it out of his mind;
phrases.notes: Both of them read ישחנה as if it were spelled with a שׂ, which gives it a new meaning.

phrases.english: and one said: let him talk it over with others.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אַמֵּי וְרַבִּי אַסִּי – חַד אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the פסוק quoted in step 14, showing it matches בן סירא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק advises getting rid of worry, either by pushing it out of one's mind or by sharing it with others.

steps.title: Maybe the problem is the line about crowds in your house
steps.stepSummary: אביי tries a fourth guess: בן סירא's advice to keep crowds out of your home and not bring everyone in.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, maybe the problem is that it says: 'Keep the many out of your house, and do not bring everyone into your house'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes another guess about the reason for the ban. This time it quotes advice about not letting too many people into your home.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This advice might sound unfriendly or against welcoming guests. The next step checks whether חז"ל taught anything like it.

phrases.english: Rather, because it is written:
"Keep the many out of your house,
and do not bring everyone into your house"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the worry guess was rejected, a new guess is offered.
steps.kashyaTarget: The permissibility of reading ספר בן סירא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Perhaps the advice to keep people out of one's home is the objectionable content.

steps.title: רבי taught the same about friends in the house
steps.stepSummary: The guess is rejected: a ברייתא records רבי teaching that a person should not bring many friends into his home, based on a פסוק in משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי also said this, as a ברייתא teaches: רבי says, a person should never have many friends inside his house, as the פסוק says: 'A man of many friends comes to harm.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the crowds guess. It shows that רבי taught the very same idea and backed it up with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי reads להתרועע as related to being broken or harmed, so too many friends can ruin a person. Since a great תנא taught the same advice from תנ"ך, it cannot be why בן סירא is banned.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
To come to harm, to be broken

phrases.english: But רבי also said it,
as it is taught: רבי says:
A person should never have many
friends inside his house,
as it is stated: "A man of many friends comes to harm."
phrases.notes: משלי 18:24

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the guess from step 16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The crowds line as a reason for the ban
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי taught the same idea in a ברייתא, based on a פסוק.

steps.title: Maybe the problem is a string of silly sayings
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes a final group of lines from בן סירא: odd sayings about beards, blowing on a cup, and asking for food to eat with bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, maybe the problem is that it says: 'A man with a thin beard is clever. A man with a thick beard is a fool. Someone who blows on his cup is not thirsty. If someone asks, "What should I eat my bread with?", take the bread away from him. Someone with a parting in his beard, the whole world cannot beat him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more guess, quoting a list of strange, silly-sounding sayings from בן סירא. This sets up the final answer, which comes right after these words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the earlier lines, these sayings have no match in תנ"ך or in the words of חז"ל. They seem like empty folk sayings with no real wisdom. Here the guesses stop being pushed away, which points to this kind of nonsense as the real reason for the ban.

keyTerms.meaning: A man with a thin, sparse beard
A man with a thick beard
A passage or parting (in the beard)

steps.whyThisMatters: After four lines (the fish, the daughters, worry, and crowds in the house) were shown to be acceptable, this list is different. Its sayings are just nonsense, and that becomes the reason not to read the book.

phrases.english: Rather, because it is written:
"A thin-bearded man is clever;
a thick-bearded man is a fool;
one who blows on his cup is not thirsty;
one who said, 'With what shall I eat bread?'
take the bread from him;
phrases.notes: The idea seems to be that if he wants something to go with his bread, he must not be really hungry.

phrases.english: one who has a parting in his beard,
the whole world cannot overcome him."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the crowds guess was rejected, a final set of lines is offered as the possible reason.
steps.kashyaTarget: The permissibility of reading ספר בן סירא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: These sayings are pointless nonsense with no source in תנ"ך or חז"ל, so they may be what makes the book unfit to read.

steps.title: The good sayings of בן סירא may still be taught
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף concludes that the excellent sayings in בן סירא may be taught, and begins quoting them, starting with lines about good and bad wives.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: The excellent sayings in בן סירא, we do teach. For example: 'A good wife is a good gift, given to a God-fearing man. A bad wife is like leprosy to her husband.' What is his fix? 'He should send her away and be healed. A beautiful wife: her husband is fortunate, and his days are doubled.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף wraps up the whole discussion about בן סירא: even though some lines are not fitting, the good lines may be taught. He starts listing examples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's first four guesses were each pushed away, but the last one, the string of silly sayings in step 18, was left standing as the reason for the ban. רב יוסף now draws the bottom line: the book as a whole is not read, but its worthwhile sayings can still be taught. The wife sayings are his first examples.

keyTerms.meaning: we teach / we explain them publicly

steps.whatToRemember: The final answer about בן סירא: we do not read the book as a whole, but we do teach its good sayings.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
The excellent things that are in it,
phrases.notes: "It" is ספר בן סירא, the book this whole discussion is about.

phrases.english: we do teach them.
"A good wife is a good gift,
she will be given into the bosom of a God-fearing man.
A bad wife is leprosy to her husband."
What is his remedy?
"He should send her away from his house
and he will be healed from his leprosy.
A beautiful wife: fortunate is her husband;
the number of his days is doubled."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: מִילֵּי מְעַלַּיְיתָא דְּאִית בֵּיהּ, דָּרְשִׁינַן לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to אביי's series of guesses (ending with step 18) by giving the final ruling on how to treat בן סירא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The book of בן סירא is not read as a whole, but its excellent sayings may be taught.

steps.title: More good advice from בן סירא: guard your eyes, home, secrets, and worries
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף continues listing worthwhile sayings of בן סירא: avoid an attractive married woman, keep crowds out of your home, share secrets with very few, and don't worry about tomorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Look away from a charming woman so you are not trapped. Don't sit drinking with her husband, because many were ruined by a beautiful woman. Those who lead people into sin cause many wounds. Like a spark lights a coal, like a cage full of birds, their houses are full of deceit. Keep crowds out of your house. Let many greet you, but tell your secret to one in a thousand. Be careful what you say even to your wife. Don't worry about tomorrow; you don't know what a day will bring. Maybe tomorrow you'll be gone, and you worried about a world that isn't yours.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps going with more examples of the good sayings from בן סירא that may be taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Notice that the line about keeping crowds out of your home is the very one אביי quoted earlier (step 16), and the advice not to worry about tomorrow is close to the worry line in step 13. Now these show up as good lines, because the earlier steps showed that the same ideas appear in משלי and in a ברייתא.
steps.confusionAlert: These are not new challenges against בן סירא. The גמרא is now quoting them as the good parts that we do teach.

phrases.english: "Turn your eyes away from a charming woman,
lest you be caught in her trap.
Do not turn aside to her husband
to mix wine and strong drink with him,
phrases.notes: He means don't become drinking buddies with her husband as an excuse to be around her.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי בְּתוֹאַר אִשָּׁה יָפָה רַבִּים הוּשְׁחָתוּ,
phrases.english: for by the looks of a beautiful woman many have been ruined,
and mighty are all those she has killed.
Many are the wounds of the peddler,
those who get people used to forbidden relations.
Like a spark lights a coal,
like a cage full of birds,
so their houses are full of deceit.
Keep the crowds out of your house,
phrases.notes: This is the same line אביי quoted back in step 16.

phrases.english: and do not bring everyone into your house.
Let many be those who ask how you are,
but reveal your secret to one in a thousand.
From the one who lies in your bosom, guard the openings of your mouth.
Do not worry about tomorrow's trouble,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי לֹא תֵדַע מַה יֵּלֶד יוֹם.
phrases.english: for you do not know what a day will bring.
Perhaps tomorrow he will be gone,

phrases.aramaic: וְנִמְצָא מִצְטַעֵר עַל עוֹלָם שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ״.
phrases.english: and it turns out he worried about a world that is not his."

steps.triggerLanguage: הַעְלֵם עֵינֶיךָ מֵאֵשֶׁת חֵן, פֶּן תִּלָּכֵד בִּמְצוּדָתָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב יוסף's list of good sayings from בן סירא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: These sayings of בן סירא (about modesty, guarding home and secrets, and not worrying) are among the worthwhile lines that may be taught.

steps.title: The poor suffer by night too
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק in משלי says all the days of the poor are bad; בן סירא adds that the nights are bad too, and describes how the poor man's roof and vineyard work against him.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'All the days of the poor are bad.' בן סירא says: 'The nights too. His roof is the lowest in town, and his vineyard is at the top of the hills. Rain from all the roofs runs down onto his roof, and the soil of his vineyard washes down into other vineyards.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another good line: בן סירא builds on a פסוק in משלי about how hard life is for a poor person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משלי speaks of the poor man's days; בן סירא adds that his nights are bad too, since he lies awake worrying. He shows why: the poor can only afford the worst spots, a low roof that collects everyone's rainwater and a hilltop vineyard whose soil washes away to others.

phrases.english: "All the days of the poor are bad."
phrases.notes: משלי 15:15

phrases.english: Ben Sira says: "The nights too.
His roof is the lowest of the roofs,
and his vineyard is at the top of the hills.
From the rain of the roofs onto his roof,
phrases.notes: The rain from everyone's higher roofs runs down onto his low roof.

phrases.english: and from the soil of his vineyard to the other vineyards."

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל יְמֵי עָנִי רָעִים. בֶּן סִירָא אוֹמֵר: אַף לֵילוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further worthwhile teaching of בן סירא, this time building on a פסוק in משלי.
steps.whatToRemember: This closes the בן סירא section: its good lines, like this one about the poor, are fit to be taught.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The poor suffer not only by day but also by night, because everything about their situation works against them.

steps.title: Memory aid for the next teachings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a list of names and key words to help remember the order of the teachings that come next.
steps.simpleTranslation: Memory aid: זירא, רבא, משרשיא, חנינא 'good,' ינאי 'nice,' יוחנן 'merciful,' יהושע 'short.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is giving a memory list of the rabbis (with a key word for some) whose teachings are about to follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is ruled here. The list helps a learner remember the order of the next statements: רבי זירא, רבא, משרשיא, then רבי חנינא about a good wife, רבי ינאי about a broad mind, רבי יוחנן about mercy, and רבי יהושע בן לוי about a narrow, impatient mind.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a teaching itself. It is just a memory list for what comes next.

phrases.english: [Memory aid: Zeira, Rava, Mesharshiyya,
phrases.notes: Some versions have this memory aid in square brackets and some don't.

phrases.english: Chanina "good," Yannai "nice,"
Yochanan "merciful," Yehoshua "short."]

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the בן סירא discussion and prepares a new series of teachings by other rabbis.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A memory list for the upcoming teachings; no ruling is given here.

steps.title: רב: The 'poor' are תלמוד scholars, the 'feasting' are משנה scholars
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא in the name of רב reads the פסוק as being about two kinds of Torah learners: בעלי תלמוד have 'bad days', and בעלי משנה have a 'constant feast'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said in the name of רב: What does the verse 'All the days of the poor are bad' mean? These are the masters of תלמוד. 'And the good-hearted has a constant feast': these are the masters of משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב takes the פסוק from משלי and applies it to two types of learners: those who learn תלמוד and those who learn משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'poor man' whose days are all bad is the בעל תלמוד. His learning is full of questions and difficulties, so he never feels settled. The בעל משנה learns the set rulings without the back-and-forth, so his learning feels like a calm, happy feast.

keyTerms.meaning: Masters of Talmud: people who dig into the reasons and the back-and-forth
Masters of משנה: people who learn the set teachings and rulings
Good-hearted, someone in a happy state

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said in the name of Rav:
What is the meaning of what is written, 'All the days of the poor are bad'?
phrases.notes: משלי 15:15, the same פסוק quoted just before.

phrases.english: These are the masters of Talmud,
'And the good-hearted has a constant feast':
these are the masters of Mishnah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the פסוק from משלי quoted in step 21 and gives it a new reading about Torah learners.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'poor' with bad days are בעלי תלמוד; the 'good-hearted' with a constant feast are בעלי משנה.

steps.title: רבא reverses the reading
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the opposite: the בעלי משנה are the ones with the bad days, and the בעלי תלמוד enjoy the feast.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said the reverse.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא disagrees with רב and flips the two groups around. This short line sets up the support for his view in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא uses the same פסוק and the same two groups but switches them. In his reading the בעל תלמוד is the happy one, and the בעל משנה is the one who suffers.

keyTerms.meaning: The reverse, the opposite way around

phrases.english: Rava said the reverse,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite reading of the same פסוק discussed in step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'poor' are בעלי משנה and the 'good-hearted' are בעלי תלמוד.

steps.title: Support for רבא from a verse in קהלת about stones and wood
steps.stepSummary: רב משרשיא quotes רבא reading a פסוק in קהלת: the stone-mover who is saddened is the בעל משנה, and the wood-chopper who is warmed is the בעל תלמוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רב משרשיא said in the name of רבא: What does the verse 'One who moves stones will be saddened by them' mean? These are the masters of משנה. 'And one who chops wood will be warmed by it'? These are the masters of תלמוד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רבא's reversed view matches another teaching of his, built on a פסוק in קהלת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Moving heavy stones is hard work that leaves you with nothing to enjoy, like the בעל משנה, who works hard but does not reach the reasoning behind the rulings. Chopping wood is also hard, but afterward you get warmth from the fire. The בעל תלמוד works hard too, and he gets to enjoy the results.

keyTerms.meaning: And this matches what someone said
One who moves or quarries stones
Read here as 'will be warmed' or 'will benefit'

steps.confusionAlert: In plain פשט, 'יסכן בם' can mean 'will be endangered by them'. Here the גמרא reads it as something good, being warmed by the wood. That is what makes it the positive half of the contrast.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא:
phrases.english: And this is what Rav Mesharshiya said in the name of Rava:
What is the meaning of what is written, 'One who moves stones will be saddened by them'?
phrases.notes: קהלת 10:9.

phrases.english: These are the masters of Mishnah.
'And one who chops wood will be warmed by it'?
These are the masters of Talmud.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רבא's reversal from step 24 with a matching teaching of his on a different פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's view that בעלי תלמוד are better off than בעלי משנה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's reading of קהלת 10:9: the saddened stone-mover is the בעל משנה, and the warmed wood-chopper is the בעל תלמוד.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: A bad wife or a good wife
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא reads the פסוק about home life: a man with a bad wife has bad days, and a man with a good wife has a constant feast.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא says: 'All the days of the poor are bad' refers to one who has a bad wife. 'And the good-hearted has a constant feast' refers to one who has a good wife.
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא gives a completely different reading of the same פסוק, this time about marriage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי חנינא, being 'poor' here is not about money or learning. A man stuck with a bad wife suffers every day, even if he is rich. A man with a good wife is always happy, as if he were at a feast.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina says:
'All the days of the poor are bad':

phrases.aramaic: – זֶה מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אִשָּׁה רָעָה.
phrases.english: this is one who has a bad wife.
'And the good-hearted has a constant feast':
this is one who has a good wife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers another reading of the same פסוק, separate from the תלמוד/משנה debate.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'poor' is one with a bad wife; the 'good-hearted' is one with a good wife.

steps.title: רבי ינאי: A picky person or an easygoing person
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי says the 'poor' is an אסטניס, someone very sensitive and easily disgusted. The 'good-hearted' is someone easygoing who isn't bothered.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי says: 'All the days of the poor are bad' refers to a delicate, sensitive person. 'And the good-hearted has a constant feast' refers to one whose mind is at ease.
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא reads the פסוק as being about personality, comparing a fussy person with a relaxed one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אסטניס is bothered by every unpleasant thing he sees or eats, so his life always feels bad. Someone whose דעתו יפה isn't fussy, so he enjoys whatever is in front of him.

keyTerms.meaning: A delicate, sensitive person who is easily disgusted
His mind is at ease; he is not fussy

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai says:
'All the days of the poor are bad': this is a delicate, sensitive person.

phrases.aramaic: ״וְטוֹב לֵב מִשְׁתֶּה תָמִיד״ – זֶה שֶׁדַּעְתּוֹ יָפָה.
phrases.english: 'And the good-hearted has a constant feast': this is one whose mind is at ease.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further reading of the same פסוק, this time about personality.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'poor' is the אסטניס; the 'good-hearted' is the easygoing person.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: A compassionate person or a cruel person
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the compassionate person has bad days, because he feels everyone's pain. The cruel person has a constant feast, because nothing bothers him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: 'All the days of the poor are bad' refers to a compassionate person. 'And the good-hearted has a constant feast' refers to a cruel person.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a surprising reading in which the kind person is the one who suffers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is not that cruelty is good. It describes how life feels. A רחמני is pained by every suffering he sees, so he is never at peace. An אכזרי doesn't care, so he goes through life feeling fine.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this as praise for being cruel. רבי יוחנן is only describing who feels at ease, not who is behaving correctly.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
'All the days of the poor are bad': this is a compassionate person.
'And the good-hearted has a constant feast': this is a cruel person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of readings of the פסוק with a reading about character.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'poor' is the compassionate person; the 'good-hearted' is the cruel person.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי begins his reading
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי starts his own reading of the פסוק. His explanation continues in the next section.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: 'All the days of the poor are bad' refers to…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens one more reading of the פסוק, this time from רבי יהושע בן לוי. His explanation continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This step only sets up his view. We hear the opening words, and the identity of the 'poor' person in his reading is given right after this.

keyTerms.meaning: A poor person; here, whoever the פסוק is really describing

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
'All the days of the poor are bad': this is…

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the next reading in the same list of interpretations.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Opening of רבי יהושע בן לוי's reading of the פסוק, which continues in the next section.
